text: Injectable medicines come in a bottle (often tinted glass to block light) sealed with a puncturable rubber cap under an aluminum seal, sometimes with a plastic tamper-evident cover; always use a clean needle (a dirty one introduces microbes/organic matter that degrade the product) and never inject air into the bottle to ease drawing up medicine, since air is not sterile. Common vial sizes are 250, 100, 50, and 20 ml. Freeze-dried (lyophilized) presentation is used mainly for live vaccines and a few medicines like Berenil for better conservation — vaccines keep only 1–2 hours after mixing with diluent, while Berenil can be kept about 7 days. Oral powder is mixed into feed or water (if soluble), an easy way to treat groups of animals; it's mainly used for premixes and preventive treatment rather than treating serious disease, since sick animals often stop eating; packaged from 100 g bags for smallholders up to 25 kg bags for commercial farms. Oral liquid requires physically dosing the animal and proper restraint; common for anti-parasitics (e.g. Albendazole in cattle) and medicines that need to act directly in the gut (e.g. piglet diarrhea or Coccidiosis treatments), usually dispensed from a pump-metered bottle. Tablets/boluses are rare for pigs and cattle (more common for dogs/cats or when farmers use human medicine) except boluses — large tablets placed directly in the uterus after delivery for antibiotic action. Eye drops are used for eye medication (other formulations irritate the eye) and for diluting chick vaccines, often tinted blue so the farmer can confirm the drop landed in the eye. Cream and spray are for local skin use, applied only to clean skin (hair cut, crusts removed, wound washed with soap and water); sprays combining disinfectant and antibiotic are useful for foot lesions (FMD, foot rot) since they can be applied at a distance without handling the animal.
